speaker: Boris Cherny
title: Head of Claude Code: What happens after coding is solved | Boris Cherny
question: In engineering organizations adopting AI agents, why does tightly budgeting or optimizing token usage too early often backfire?
guest: My advice generally is don't try to optimize or cost-cut at the beginning. Start by giving engineers as many tokens as possible. We're starting to see unlimited tokens come up as a perk at some companies, and I very much encourage it because it makes people free to try ideas that would have been too crazy. At small scale, you're not going to get a giant bill. If it's an individual engineer experimenting, the token cost is still relatively low compared to their salary or other costs of running the business. So it's actually not a huge cost early on. Then if there's an idea that works and scales up—say they build something awesome that takes a huge amount of tokens and the cost becomes pretty big—that's the point to optimize and cost-cut, and figure out if you can run it with a smaller model like Haiku or Sonnet instead of Opus. Just don't do that too early.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Tightly budgeting tokens early backfires because it optimizes the cheapest, most visible input before the organization has learned where agents actually create value. Token spend is usually small next to engineer salaries and the cost of delayed delivery, so caps save pennies while suppressing the experimentation that reveals high-leverage workflows.

Early constraints also degrade results in ways that get misattributed. Starving agents of context, forcing smaller models, or limiting iterations and verification passes produces worse output, more human rework, and failed tasks. Teams then conclude that "agents don't work" when the real problem was the budget. Engineers respond to quotas by rationing use, avoiding ambitious tasks, and falling back on manual work, which stalls skill-building and adoption.

There is also a timing problem: usage patterns, model prices, and capabilities shift quickly, so early optimizations target a moving baseline and often lock in brittle workarounds. Per-token prices have tended to fall, making premature efficiency work poor-return engineering.

The better sequence is to measure usage, find what delivers outcomes, and then optimize cost per successful task rather than raw tokens, using sensible guardrails against runaway spend instead of tight caps.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Tightly budgeting or optimizing token usage too early trades cheap compute for expensive engineering time while obscuring what AI agents can actually do. Effective software agents depend on rich context: reading surrounding files, tracing dependencies, reasoning through edge cases, and iterating against test failures. Capping context windows, model tiers, or tool-call turns starves agents of the information needed to succeed, turning reliable automation into brittle guesswork. That false economy quickly multiplies costs, as engineers burn hours reviewing and fixing flawed patches or re-running failed tasks—often spending more total tokens across retries than one unconstrained run would have used. Premature limits also poison adoption: developers conclude that agents are unreliable when they are simply under-provisioned, stalling experimentation before high-leverage workflows emerge. Meanwhile, falling inference prices and stronger models rapidly turn custom token-saving hacks into maintenance debt. Engineering teams get far better returns by proving reliability and workflow value at full capability first, then optimizing unit economics once usage patterns stabilize.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Clamping down on token spend too early usually saves money in the wrong place. Early on, the costly part isn't tokens, it's engineers' time and what the organization hasn't learned yet. Agents do their best work when they get plenty of context, can explore a codebase, run tests, retry, and check their own output. If you starve them with small context windows, cheaper models or hard caps, the code they produce is worse. People then spend hours fixing it and conclude that "AI doesn't work here," often from a test that was rigged against it.

Budgets also discourage the experiments adoption depends on. Engineers won't try ambitious workflows like parallel agents, long-running tasks or automated review when every run feels like a cost to justify. Nobody finds out which uses pay off, so there's nothing useful to optimize later. Early usage patterns are noisy and change quickly as models and prices move, so tuning around them locks in today's habits. A sounder order is to encourage heavy use first, measure results such as cycle time and quality, and optimize once you know which usage creates value.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Tightly budgeting or optimizing token usage too early backfires because early AI agent adoption is primarily a learning and workflow-discovery phase, not a cost-minimization phase. When organizations impose strict caps upfront, engineers hesitate to experiment, ration agent runs, or revert to manual work to avoid hitting limits, stalling adoption before teams learn where agents deliver real leverage.

It also creates a false economy. Token spend is typically trivial compared to engineering salaries, so forcing developers to micromanage prompts, strip down context, or switch prematurely to weaker models saves pennies in compute while wasting hours of expensive human time. Worse, starving agents of context, reasoning steps, or retry loops degrades output quality, shifting the burden onto engineers through extra debugging, rework, and review cycles, which often consumes even more tokens and time.

Finally, you cannot optimize what you have not yet validated. Organizations get far better returns by first letting teams discover high-impact workflows and tuning token efficiency only after usage patterns and outcomes are clear.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Tight token budgets can make each agent run cheaper while making the work more expensive. Early in adoption, teams are still learning which tasks agents handle well and how much context, iteration, and verification those tasks need. A cap can push an agent to stop before running tests or investigating a failure, shifting the cost to retries, human review, and rework. It can also make a promising workflow look unviable because the team never sees what it can do with enough room to work.

Use spending guardrails to catch runaway costs, then measure the cost per successfully completed task, including human time. Once a workflow reliably produces good results, optimize the parts that consume tokens without improving the outcome.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Token usage is easy to measure, but it’s a poor proxy for the cost of getting engineering work done. A tight budget can make an agent skip context it needs, stop before it tests a change, or hand unfinished work back to an engineer. A cheaper run can then mean more retries, longer reviews, and a higher total cost per completed task.

Early on, teams are still learning which tasks agents handle well and where an extra round of investigation or testing saves human time. Strict limits can cut off the experiments that reveal those patterns. A better starting point is to set spending guardrails and track cost per successfully completed task alongside quality and engineer time. Once those patterns are clear, teams can target waste without cutting the work that makes the agent valuable.
